region: Shared Yayoi archaeological history for the exact 400 to 323 BCE and 100 to 200 CE atlas records
researcher: Codex parallel release159-yayoi-shared research, integrated by Codex

sources.title: Human History Map civilization index
sources.note: Exact live ids, identical display names, approximate intervals, and generated-source fields for yayoi and yayoi-100.

sources.title: Human History Map imported summaries
sources.note: Identical imported Yayoi-period summary and source lead attached to both exact ids.

sources.title: Human History Map coverage registry
sources.note: Two missing-card records, one observed border interval each, and pending identity, chronology, and border review.

sources.title: Human History Map missing-card registry
sources.note: Queue entries showing both exact Yayoi ids lack staged or runtime cards.

sources.title: Human History Map card index
sources.note: Direct check that neither exact Yayoi id has an indexed runtime card before integration.

sources.title: Human History Map 500 to 400 BCE borders
sources.note: Exact pre-start seam control for the earlier yayoi feature.

sources.title: Human History Map 400 to 323 BCE borders
sources.note: Only exact yayoi feature, decoded geometry, shared arc, representative membership, and overlap diagnostics.

sources.title: Human History Map 323 to 300 BCE borders
sources.note: Exact post-end seam control showing the earlier id absent.

sources.title: Human History Map 1 BCE to 100 CE borders
sources.note: Exact pre-start seam control for yayoi-100 and evidence that the atlas gap continues through 100 CE.

sources.title: Human History Map 100 to 200 CE borders
sources.note: Only exact yayoi-100 feature, decoded geometry, representative membership, and overlap diagnostics.

sources.title: Human History Map 200 to 300 CE borders
sources.note: Exact endpoint control showing yayoi-100 absent even while late Yayoi history continues.

sources.title: What Is Yayoi Culture?
sources.note: National Museum of Japanese History exhibition outline on long chronology, wet-field farming, regional diversity, and coexistence with other archaeological cultures.

sources.title: Japan Considered from the Farmer and Language Spread Hypothesis
sources.note: Peer-reviewed synthesis emphasizing that Yayoi is a Japanese period designation spanning farmers, hunter-gatherers, and a time-transgressive regional transition.

sources.title: Introduction to Japanese Archaeology and Protohistory
sources.note: Academic introduction separating archaeological Yayoi from Wa polities known through Chinese texts and placing substantial written evidence in the third century.

sources.title: Formation and Development of Agrarian Society
sources.note: National Museum of Japanese History research summary on tenth-century-BCE paddy farming, slow spread, stone tools, iron timing, settlement counts, and regional chronologies.

sources.title: The History of Yoshinogari
sources.note: Official park account distinguishing early, middle, and late Yayoi settlement, moats, burial jars, leader mounds, defenses, and large buildings.

sources.title: Moat-Encircled Village Zone
sources.note: Official park inventory of public dwellings, storehouses, workshop and ceremonial areas, cooking house, and authentic burial jars.

sources.title: Yayoi Trivia
sources.note: Official park evidence and interpretation on foods, child burial jars, springs and wells, missing restroom remains, comparison-site parasites, and the site’s later desertion.

sources.title: Southern Inner Enclosure
sources.note: Official park interpretation of elite residences, pit dwellings, iron finds, watchtowers, defenses, and status differences at late Yayoi Yoshinogari.

sources.title: Excavation and Reconstruction at Yoshinogari
sources.note: Official explanation that reconstructions were developed through excavation plus comparison with Japanese, Korean, and Chinese archaeological sites.

sources.title: Grain Storehouses at Yoshinogari
sources.note: Official mobile guide identifying entrance-area raised storehouses as places for ears of rice used as food.

sources.title: The World of the Gold Seal and the Age of Nakoku
sources.note: Fukuoka City Museum bilingual guide on the five-character seal, its 1784 Shikanoshima discovery, the 57 CE Later Han grant, Nakoku, and Itazuke agriculture.

sources.title: Government Offices and Seals
sources.note: Fukuoka City Museum page giving the official object title, characters, Japanese reading Kan no Wa no Na no Kokuo, and 57 CE date.

sources.title: Foundations of Nakoku
sources.note: Fukuoka City Museum archaeological synthesis of early northern Kyushu settlements, Itazuke fields, canals, storage pits, Korean Peninsula connections, and layered traditions.

sources.title: The Age of Yayoi Pottery
sources.note: Fukuoka City Museum discussion of jar sizes, rice storage, storage pits, declining shallow bowls, and changing food practices.

sources.title: The Sea and Archaeological Sites in the Yayoi Period
sources.note: Fukuoka City Museum archaeological account of coastal fishing settlements, hooks, net weights, salt-making pottery, cemeteries, and exchange.

sources.title: History of the Kingdom of Wei on Wa and Queen Pimiko
sources.note: Columbia University licensed translation of the circa-297 Wei history on Wa communities, envoys and scribes, clothing and status, conflict, Himiko, and her household.

sources.title: History of the Kingdom of Wei on Wa and Queen Pimiko, classroom PDF
sources.note: Columbia University primary-source PDF carrying the translated passage on Wa envoys and scribes and the document-based teaching context.

sources.title: The Household as a Node of Communal Collaboration
sources.note: Peer-reviewed northern Kyushu case study defining a recurring basic unit of about five houses, shared storage, and a burial ground while examining cooperation and tension.

sources.title: Dental Morbid Condition of Yayoi Agriculturalists
sources.note: Peer-reviewed comparison finding more caries and periodontal indicators among northern Kyushu agriculturalists than comparison hunter-gatherers, with sample and inference limits.

sources.title: Deciduous Dental Caries in Japanese Children
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study citing the only reported Yayoi deciduous-tooth sample, numerical caries rates, and missing site and subsistence context.

sources.title: Population Pressure and Prehistoric Violence in the Yayoi Period
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study of middle Yayoi jar burials and skeletal trauma, including regional clustering and a bounded statistical association with population pressure.

sources.title: Chronology of Yayoi Skeletal Remains from Kanto
sources.note: Peer-reviewed radiocarbon reassessment showing collections labeled Yayoi can contain Jomon, Yayoi, and Kofun remains and require specimen-level dating.

sources.title: Ancient Genomes from Northwestern Kyushu Yayoi
sources.note: Peer-reviewed ancient-DNA study reporting genetic diversity, tested kinship coefficients, and gradual admixture rather than a single uniform migration event.

sources.title: Yayoi Jar-Coffin and Pit Burials at Takuta-Nishibun
sources.note: Japanese bioarchaeology project on two contemporaneous burial groups and genome analysis, useful for separating burial form from assumed identity or rank.

sources.title: Kyushu National Museum Cultural Exchange Hall
sources.note: National museum overview of continental connections bringing wet-rice cultivation and bronze and iron techniques during the Yayoi period.

sources.title: Himiko and Her Mirrors
sources.note: Kyushu National Museum exhibition account of Himiko’s 239 CE envoy, Wei’s gift of one hundred mirrors, and later political uses, presented with attribution.

sources.title: Local Societies from Yayoi to Early Kofun
sources.note: National Museum of Japanese History research on Kinki bronze and iron production and continuities across the Yayoi-to-Kofun transition.

sources.title: Dotaku and the Yayoi Period
sources.note: Kyoto National Museum introduction to ritual bronze bells, their changing form and use, farming imagery, and Yayoi agricultural society.

sources.title: Kofun Colours: Decorated Japanese Tumuli
sources.note: Kyushu National Museum explanation of third- to seventh-century Kofun tombs, their varied forms, and the famous keyhole type.
